title: The Eye of the Sahara
hook: A giant stone bullseye in the Sahara looks like an impact crater, but it isn't one.
peek: In the desert of Mauritania sits a set of rings 40 to 50 kilometres across, so clear from orbit that astronauts used it as a landmark. It looks like the scar of a meteorite, but it was made by slow uplift and wind and water.
lede: The Richat Structure in Mauritania is hard to notice from the ground, where it just looks like rocky desert. From space it is a near perfect set of concentric rings 40 to 50 kilometres across. Early astronauts used it as a landmark, and many people assumed it was an impact crater. Geologists found no sign of an impact at all.

bullets.text: Because it stands out so sharply against the flat sands, the Eye of the Sahara became a familiar sight for crews from the Gemini missions of the 1960s onward, who used it to get their bearings.
A meteorite strike leaves shocked minerals and melted rock, and the Richat has neither. Its centre is also flat rather than a bowl, which ruled out the crater idea.
Geologists think molten rock pushed the ground up into a dome roughly 100 million years ago. Erosion then sliced off the top, exposing rings of hard and soft rock that wear away at different speeds.
Online videos sometimes claim the rings are the lost city of Atlantis. Geologists see nothing to support this: the rings are natural rock layers, formed long before any people existed.
